summary: Sheikh Ali Mashhour discusses the concept of Hijrah (migration) in Islamic jurisprudence as part of his commentary on Zadul-Ma'ad. He explains that Hijrah linguistically means to abandon or leave something, and in Islamic law refers to leaving a place where one cannot openly practice Islam. The sheikh clarifies that Hijrah was not obligatory in the early years of prophethood but became mandatory around the tenth year. He details the minimum requirements for obligatory migration: the ability to openly profess Islam, establish prayer, fast during Ramadan, and perform Hajj. The lecture then transitions to the historical context of the Prophet's efforts to call tribes to Islam during the seasonal markets and Hajj seasons in Mecca, describing how the Quraysh nobility, particularly Abu Lahab, actively opposed and undermined the Prophet's message despite his consistent efforts to invite people to Islam.
